note: State income tax at a glance. Withholding formulas themselves stay in the site's code; what is here are the published rates, notes and the authority each state publishes them in.

states.name: Texas
notes: Texas has no state income tax, and nothing else is withheld at state level either.
Your paycheck is shaped entirely by federal withholding and FICA.
Texas employers pay unemployment insurance, but it does not come out of your pay.

states.name: Florida
notes: Florida has no state income tax and no state-level payroll deduction from your pay.
Reemployment tax is paid by employers, not withheld from wages.

states.name: Washington
notes: Washington has no state income tax.
Two state programs are still withheld from your pay: Paid Family & Medical Leave and WA Cares.
changesForYear: The Paid Family & Medical Leave premium rose from 0.92% to 1.13% of wages.

states.name: Tennessee
notes: Tennessee has no tax on wage income.
The Hall income tax on interest and dividends was fully repealed in 2021, so wages are untouched at state level.

states.name: Nevada
notes: Nevada has no state income tax.
The Modified Business Tax is paid by employers, not withheld from your pay.

states.name: Wyoming
notes: Wyoming has no state income tax and no employee payroll deduction.
Only federal withholding and FICA come out of your pay.

states.name: South Dakota
notes: South Dakota has no state income tax and no employee-side payroll deduction.
Unemployment insurance is paid by employers only.

states.name: New Hampshire
notes: New Hampshire does not tax wages.
Its old tax on interest and dividends ended after 2024, so there is nothing left that touches a paycheck.

states.name: Alaska
notes: Alaska has no state income tax.
It is one of the very few states where employees pay into unemployment insurance: 0.5% of wages up to $54,200, so at most $271 a year.
That is the only state-level deduction on an Alaska paycheck.
changesForYear: The unemployment wage base rose to $54,200, lifting the maximum employee contribution to $271.

states.name: Illinois
notes: Illinois taxes income at a flat 4.95%.
Each exemption on your IL-W-4 takes $2,925 off the income that rate applies to.
Illinois does not tax retirement income — pensions, 401(k) withdrawals and Social Security are all exempt.

states.name: Georgia
notes: Georgia taxes income at a flat 4.99%, cut from 5.19% by HB 463 in May 2026.
The standard deduction went up at the same time: $15,000 for a single filer, $30,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
Each dependent takes another $5,000 off the taxable amount.
The rate cut is backdated to 1 January 2026, but employers only had to start withholding at 4.99% from 11 May — so pay stubs from early in the year may show the old rate.
changesForYear: HB 463 cut the flat rate from 5.19% to 4.99%, effective for withholding from 11 May 2026.
The standard deduction rose from $12,000 to $15,000 for single filers, and the dependent deduction from $4,000 to $5,000.

states.name: Wisconsin
notes: Wisconsin's income tax rates are 3.5%, 4.4%, 5.3% and 7.65% — the bottom two were cut by Act 19 back in 2023.
The withholding tables your employer uses were not updated to match. They still date from 1 January 2022 and use the older 3.54% and 4.65% for the lower bands.
So Wisconsin takes slightly more out of each paycheck than you finally owe, and the difference comes back at filing time.
Its standard deduction shrinks as you earn more: a single filer gets $6,702 below $17,780, and nothing at all above $73,630.
That taper is why the share of your pay going to Wisconsin climbs faster than the bracket rates alone suggest.

states.name: Virginia
notes: Virginia has four income tax rates, from 2% up to 5.75%.
The top 5.75% rate starts at just $17,000 of taxable income, so nearly everyone reaches it — the lower bands barely matter.
The standard deduction is $8,750 for a single filer, plus $930 for each personal exemption.

states.name: Iowa
notes: Iowa taxes income at a flat 3.8%, after a standard deduction of $13,000 for a single filer.
Each allowance is worth $40 off the tax itself, not off your income — Iowa is unusual in doing it that way.
Iowa no longer taxes retirement income for anyone aged 55 or over.

states.name: Colorado
notes: Colorado taxes income at a flat 4.4%, after a standard deduction of $5,500 for a single filer.
Colorado dropped numbered allowances entirely — the DR 0004 form uses wage brackets and dependent counts instead.

states.name: North Carolina
notes: North Carolina withholds at a flat 4.09% — slightly above its 3.99% income tax rate.
That gap is deliberate: the state withholds a little extra so most people do not end up owing at filing.
The standard deduction is $12,750, plus $2,500 for each dependent.

states.name: Pennsylvania
notes: Pennsylvania taxes wages at a flat 3.07% — with no standard deduction, no personal exemption and no allowances.
It is the simplest state withholding formula in the country: 3.07% of everything you earn.
Most Pennsylvania towns add a local Earned Income Tax on top, usually 1% to 3%, which is not included here.

states.name: Oklahoma
notes: Oklahoma has three rates — 2.5%, 3.5% and 4.5% — but the bands are narrow.
The first $10,100 is taxed at 0% for a single filer, and the top 4.5% rate starts at just $13,550, so almost everyone lands there.
Each exemption on your OK-W-4 takes $1,000 off the taxable amount.

states.name: Arizona
notes: Arizona is unusual: you pick your own withholding rate on Form A-4, from 0.5% to 3.5% in half-point steps.
If you never filed an A-4, your employer withholds at 2.0% — that is the figure used here.
Arizona's actual income tax rate is a flat 2.5%, so the 2.0% default withholds less than you owe and can leave a small bill at filing time.
Picking 2.5% on your A-4 is the closest match to what you will actually owe.

states.name: Louisiana
notes: Louisiana withholds at a flat 3.09%, slightly above its 3% income tax rate.
A single filer gets a $12,500 personal exemption before that rate applies, and $25,000 if married filing jointly.
Each dependent takes another $1,000 off.

states.name: Indiana
notes: Indiana taxes income at a flat 2.95%, one of the lowest state rates in the country.
Each exemption on your WH-4 takes $1,000 off the taxable amount.
Every Indiana county adds its own income tax on top, from 0.5% to 3.0% — that is not included here, and in some counties it is larger than the state tax itself.

states.name: Kentucky
notes: Kentucky taxes income at a flat 3.5%, after a standard deduction of $3,360.
That deduction is the same whatever your filing status — Kentucky does not raise it for married couples.
Many Kentucky cities and counties add a local occupational tax on wages, typically 1% to 2.5%, which is not included here.

states.name: Missouri
notes: Missouri has eight tax bands, but they are extremely narrow — the top 4.7% rate starts at just $9,436 of taxable income.
The standard deduction matches the federal one: $16,100 for a single filer.
Missouri used to let you deduct federal tax paid before applying its own rates. That step was removed for 2026.
changesForYear: Missouri removed the federal income tax deduction from its withholding formula.

states.name: Maine
notes: Maine has three tax bands, from 5.8% up to 7.15% — the lowest band already starts higher than many states' top rate.
Each allowance takes $5,300 off your taxable pay, on top of a $12,450 standard deduction for a single filer.
That standard deduction tapers away between $102,250 and $177,250 of income, and disappears entirely above it.

states.name: Idaho
notes: Idaho taxes income at a single flat rate of 5.3%, down from 5.695% the year before.
The first $15,000 you earn is taxed at 0% ($30,000 if married filing jointly), so the effective rate is lower than 5.3%.
Idaho dropped personal and spousal allowances — only dependents reduce withholding, at $3,868 each.
changesForYear: Idaho cut its flat income tax rate from 5.695% to 5.3%.

states.name: Michigan
notes: Michigan taxes income at a flat 4.25%.
Each personal exemption on your MI-W4 takes $5,900 off the income that rate applies to.
Some Michigan cities add their own income tax on top — Detroit charges 2.4% for residents.
changesForYear: The Michigan personal exemption rose from $5,800 to $5,900.

states.name: Minnesota
notes: Minnesota has four income tax rates, from 5.35% up to 9.85%.
Each withholding allowance on your W-4MN takes $5,300 off the income those rates apply to.
The top 9.85% rate only starts above $207,850 for a single filer, so most people never reach it.

states.name: Montana
notes: Montana has two income tax rates: 4.7% and 5.65%.
The first $16,100 you earn is taxed at 0% for a single filer — Montana uses the same standard deduction as the federal return.
The 5.65% rate only applies to income above $63,600 for a single filer.
changesForYear: HB 337 cut Montana's top rate from 5.9% to 5.65% from 1 January 2026.

states.name: Mississippi
notes: Mississippi taxes income at 4% — but only above $10,000 of taxable pay. The first $10,000 is taxed at 0%.
A single filer also gets a $2,300 standard deduction and a $6,000 personal exemption before that.
The rate is on a legislated path down to 3% by 2030, cut from 4.4% to 4% for 2026.
changesForYear: Mississippi cut its rate from 4.4% to 4% for 2026, on the way to 3% by 2030.

states.name: Utah
notes: Utah taxes income at a flat 4.5% of everything you earn — there is no standard deduction to subtract first.
Instead there is a small withholding allowance, $450 for a single filer, and it tapers away as income rises.
Above roughly $19,000 a year the allowance is gone entirely, so most people pay the full 4.5%.

states.name: South Carolina
notes: South Carolina has two rates that bite — 3% and 6% — plus a 0% band on the first $3,640.
The 6% rate starts at $18,230 of taxable pay, so most full-time workers reach it.
The standard deduction is 10% of your wages, capped at $7,500, and each exemption takes another $4,860 off.

states.name: Alabama
notes: Alabama has three rates — 2%, 4% and 5% — but the bands are tiny: the top 5% starts at just $3,000 of taxable income.
The standard deduction shrinks as you earn more, from $3,000 down to a floor of $2,500 above $35,500 of wages.
A single filer also gets a $1,500 personal exemption.
Many Alabama cities charge an occupational tax on wages, typically 1% to 2%, which is not included here.

states.name: Kansas
notes: Kansas has two rates, 5.2% and 5.58%, on top of a 0% band covering the first $3,605 for a single filer.
The higher rate starts at $23,000 above that band, so most full-time workers pay some of it.
Each exemption on your K-4 takes $2,320 off the taxable amount.

states.name: North Dakota
notes: North Dakota has the gentlest income tax of any state that charges one: 1.95% and 2.5%.
The first $57,625 a single filer earns is taxed at 0% — so on a typical salary the state takes only a few dollars a paycheck.
The 2.5% top rate does not start until $258,450, which almost nobody reaches.
If you filed a 2020 or later W-4, North Dakota uses your federal taxable wages directly with no state allowance.

states.name: Vermont
notes: Vermont has four rates — 3.35%, 6.6%, 7.6% and 8.75% — on top of a 0% band covering the first $3,925.
Each exemption you claim takes $5,400 off before the rates apply, which is one of the more generous allowances in the country.
The 6.6% rate does not start until $54,675 of taxable pay, so a typical salary stays mostly in the 3.35% band.

states.name: Delaware
notes: Delaware has six rates from 2.2% to 6.6%, but the bands are narrow — the top 6.6% rate starts at just $60,000.
The standard deduction is $3,250 for a single filer, well below the federal one.
Each allowance is worth $110 off the tax itself, not off your income — Delaware works like Iowa in that respect.
If you work in Wilmington, the city adds a 1.25% wage tax that is not included here.

states.name: Rhode Island
notes: Rhode Island has three rates — 3.75%, 4.75% and 5.99% — and no 0% band, so the tax starts on the first dollar.
The 4.75% rate does not start until $82,050, so most workers stay in the bottom band.
Each exemption is worth $1,000, but the allowance disappears entirely once wages pass $290,800.

states.name: Massachusetts
notes: Massachusetts taxes income at a flat 5%, plus a 4% surtax on earnings above $1,107,750 — the so-called millionaire's tax.
A single filer gets a $4,400 exemption; each extra exemption adds $1,000 to a $3,400 base.
Massachusetts also lets you deduct the Social Security and Medicare tax you paid, up to $2,000 a year — almost no other state does this.
If you claim an exemption and earn under $8,000 a year, nothing is withheld at all.

states.name: Hawaii
notes: Hawaii has eight rates, from 1.4% up to 7.9%, and the bands are narrow — a single filer reaches 7.6% at $48,000.
There is no standard deduction in the withholding formula; each allowance you claim is worth $1,144.
Hawaii is phasing in wider brackets through 2031, so what your employer withholds may differ from what your annual return works out to.

states.name: New Jersey
notes: New Jersey has seven rates from 1.5% to 11.8%, and the bands jump sharply: 3.9% at $35,000, then 6.1% at $40,000.
Each exemption you claim is worth $1,000 off your taxable pay.
Three separate contributions also come out of a New Jersey paycheck — unemployment, temporary disability and family leave.
Disability and family leave both dropped for 2026: TDI from 0.23% to 0.19%, FLI from 0.33% to 0.23%.
changesForYear: Temporary Disability fell from 0.23% to 0.19% and Family Leave from 0.33% to 0.23%, while the wage base for both rose to $171,100.

states.name: Ohio
notes: Ohio's income tax is a flat 2.75% on income above $26,050, but the tables your employer uses to withhold are not flat — they run 1.6%, 2.99% and 3.4%.
That is deliberate: withholding only subtracts a $650 exemption, not the $26,050 the tax itself exempts, so the rates are set to compensate.
The practical effect is that what comes out of your paycheck and what you finally owe are worked out two different ways.
Many Ohio cities and school districts levy their own income tax, often 1% to 2.5%, which is not included here.
changesForYear: New withholding tables took effect for pay periods ending on or after 1 August 2026, replacing rates of 1.775%, 2.99% and 3.64%.

states.name: Nebraska
notes: Nebraska's withholding table has seven bands, from 2.26% up to 4.6%, on top of a 0% band covering the first $3,430.
Each allowance you claim is worth $2,440 off your taxable pay — one of the larger allowances in the country.
The withholding table has more bands than the income tax itself, which the state is phasing down separately, so the two do not line up exactly.
If you claim enough allowances to push withholding very low, a state rule (LB 223) sets a floor on what your employer must still take out.

states.name: West Virginia
notes: West Virginia cut every rate again for 2026: the top rate is now 4.58%, down from 4.82%.
The cut was signed on 12 June 2026 but applies retroactively to 1 January, so withholding changed part-way through the year.
Each exemption you claim is worth $2,000 off your taxable pay.
The same five bands apply whether you file single or jointly — West Virginia does not widen them for couples.
changesForYear: Senate Bill 392 cut all five rates by about 5%: 2.22% to 2.11%, 2.96% to 2.81%, 3.33% to 3.16%, 4.44% to 4.22% and 4.82% to 4.58%.

states.name: Arkansas
notes: Arkansas cut its top rate to 3.7% for 2026 — the fourth cut in four years.
The first $5,600 you earn is taxed at 0%, and the standard deduction takes another $2,470 off before that.
Each exemption is worth $29 off the tax itself, not off your income.
Above $94,700 Arkansas switches to a different, simpler table, and the tax jumps at that point rather than easing in.
changesForYear: The top rate fell from 3.9% to 3.7%, signed on 6 May 2026 and applied retroactively to 1 January.

states.name: California
notes: California has ten withholding bands, from 1.1% up to 14.63% — the widest spread of any state.
Those withholding rates sit above the headline income tax rates because the 1% mental health surcharge is folded into them.
State Disability Insurance takes another 1.3% of your pay, and since 2024 there is no wage cap on it — high earners pay it on every dollar.
Each allowance is worth $163.90 off the tax itself, and the standard deduction doubles to $11,412 once you claim two or more.
Earn under $18,368 as a single filer and California withholds nothing at all.
changesForYear: State Disability Insurance rose from 1.2% to 1.3% of wages on 1 January 2026, with no wage cap.

states.name: New York
notes: New York's withholding table has thirteen bands, and the rates do not simply climb — they dip and spike.
That is deliberate: bands at 11.44% claw back the benefit of the lower rates from high earners, so the average rate lands where the state wants it.
A single filer gets $7,400 off the top, plus $1,000 for each allowance claimed.
If you live in New York City, the city charges its own income tax on top of this, roughly 3.1% to 3.9%, which is not included here.
New York also deducts Paid Family Leave from your pay — a small percentage set each year, which this calculator does not include.

states.name: Oregon
notes: Oregon is the only state that lets you subtract the federal tax you paid before working out state tax — up to $8,750 a year.
That subtraction is why Oregon's rates look steep but the amount taken is lower than you would expect: 8.75% applies to what is left after federal tax comes off.
There is no sales tax in Oregon, which is the trade-off for income tax rates starting at 4.75%.
A statewide transit tax of 0.1% also comes out of every paycheck.
The federal subtraction and the $263 personal credit both phase out for higher earners; this calculator switches them off above the thresholds rather than tapering them.

states.name: Maryland
notes: Maryland is really two taxes: the state's own rates from 2% to 5.75%, plus a county tax that comes out of the same paycheck.
County rates run from 2.25% to 3.30% for 2026. This calculator uses 3.20%, near the top of that range.
If your county charges less, your take-home is higher than shown; the gap between the lowest and highest county is just under 1% of your taxable pay.
The standard deduction is 15% of your income but capped at $2,550 for a single filer, so almost everyone gets the cap.
Each exemption is worth another $3,200 off.

states.name: Connecticut
notes: Connecticut works out withholding in five stages, and no other state stacks this many.
First an exemption comes off — $15,000 for a single filer, shrinking $1,000 for every $1,000 you earn over $30,000 and gone above $44,000.
Then the rates apply, from 2% up to 6.99%.
Then two amounts get added back: a phase-out charge above $56,500 that claws back the 2% band, and a recapture charge above $105,000 that claws back the lower rates entirely.
Finally a personal credit cuts the whole result — 75% at the bottom, tapering to nothing once you pass $64,500.
The effect is that two people $5,000 apart in salary can face noticeably different rates, which is why Connecticut paycheck maths surprises people.

states.name: New Mexico
notes: New Mexico has six rates, from 1.5% up to 5.9%, and the first $8,050 a single filer earns is not taxed at all.
There is no state allowance to claim if you filed a 2020 or later W-4 — New Mexico works straight from your federal taxable wages.
The bands for a married couple are exactly double the single ones at the bottom, but not at the top: 5.9% starts at $218,050 single and $331,100 jointly.
Bonuses and other supplemental pay are withheld at a flat 5.9%.
